speaker_role: independent counselor (founder of a paid admissions consultancy, Harvard graduate; not a former admissions officer himself, though he says his firm employs one)
commercial_incentive: Yes - actively promotes his consultancy (Endurable) with a referral discount code for the host's viewers
key_insights: Many top colleges use an internal point/category system (e.g., academics, athletics, extracurriculars, personal factors) to rank applicants rather than a single holistic score
Admissions review is framed as two questions: is the student qualified to succeed academically, and then is the student distinctively 'special' relative to other qualified applicants
He argues true elite-school odds are closer to 3-4% of the top 10% of a school's student body, not 3-4% of all applicants, implying the real competition is much fiercer than raw admit rates suggest
Recommends taking the hardest available courses (AP/honors) over easier classes with higher grades, since admissions readers at selective schools can tell the difference
For test-optional decisions, advises submitting scores if strong, but says the calculus depends on the student's access to testing resources, not just the raw score
If weak in one area (e.g., test scores), the application should show clear excellence in another area to compensate
Says essays and recommendation letters carry more weight at the most selective schools because they reveal how a student thinks and what they prioritize

Advises against essays that read as pure complaint/victimhood; frames challenges instead as something the student actively worked through, using a Tesla-vs-competitors analogy about attitude under adversity
specific_numbers_or_facts: Jason (the guest) claims his firm's first client, a student from central China with a 1320 SAT, was one of only 8 Chinese admits to Harvard that year
Jason states top schools like Harvard/Yale/Stanford/Princeton/MIT have roughly 3-4% admit rates
Jason claims his firm became the #1 ranked company for sending Chinese students to Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Princeton, MIT, and Caltech in its fourth year
Amy Wang (host) offers viewers a $500 discount on the consultancy's services via a referral code
notable_or_distinctive: The framing of elite admissions odds as '3-4% of the top 10%' rather than the headline admit rate is a more analytically interesting way of contextualizing selectivity than typical generic advice.
reliability_notes: This is a paid-consultancy promotional interview; claims about the firm's results (e.g., 'only 8 admissions from all of China,' '#1 ranked company') are self-reported and unverifiable, and general advice is asserted without citing specific admissions-office sources.
